New single “Ain’t Got Time” supplies it in abundance. Over an understated soul loop that feels like a smoky room, Bruiser applies his cartoonish enunciation to a subject worthy of key inspiration…
entry.content:
When the distinctive Detroit emcee Bruiser Wolf and the boom-bap producer Conductor Williams team up, you know exactly what you're going to get. New single "Ain't Got Time" supplies it in abundance. Over an understated soul loop that feels like a smoky room, Bruiser applies his cartoonish enunciation to a subject worthy of key inspiration Too $hort: He's got money, not time, and he doesn't care if you love him, he just wants you to fuck him. It's over in under two minutes — the song, not the sex, though who can say for sure about the latter.

Watch the Diego-directed video below.

entry.title: The 5 Best Songs Of The Week
entry.summary: Every week the Stereogum staff chooses the five best new songs of the week. The eligibility period begins and ends Thursdays right before midnight. You can hear this week’s picks below and on Stereogum’s Favorite New Music Spotify playlist, which is updated weekly. (An expanded playlist of our new music picks is available to subscribers on Spotify and Apple…
entry.content:
Every week the Stereogum staff chooses the five best new songs of the week. The eligibility period begins and ends Thursdays right before midnight. You can hear this week’s picks below and on Stereogum’s Favorite New Music Spotify playlist, which is updated weekly. (An expanded playlist of our new music picks is available to subscribers on Spotify and Apple Music, updated throughout the week.)

5

Worldpeace DMT - "Ringtone"

A band this distinctively 2000s making a love song about ringtones may be a little on the nose, but when it's this catchy, this charming, this seamless in its blend of the elegant and chintzy? On sophomore album Stick Around For Tea, Worldpeace DMT are digging back into the blog-era moment when twee, in all its childlike wonder, got a cyborg infusion. On "Ringtone," we hear them in anthem mode, giving spotlight moments to so many little ingredients but never letting the details get in the way of that hook about the search for God, love, and world peace. What a cute little tune about some of the biggest subjects imaginable. —Chris

4

sadie - "Little Things"

Don’t overthink it. On her bright new single "Little Things," sadie reminds us of the world outside of our heads. "Won't you come and get me out of my mind," she sings over galloping drums and heavenly synth bloops. “Little Things” is bliss and curiosity bottled in sound: Strings take deep breaths, backing tracks reverse into the ether, and a bass line sounds like it’s hopping across lily pads. sadie creates this feeling that everything earthbound is magic. And it is! What if everything just glowed — whether it was the way the light hits the shoulders of a tree or fresh piss on the city streets. It’s easy to forget what a joy it is to experience this crazy world. —Margaret

3

Hannah Frances - "Circadian Heart"

Hannah Frances says "Circadian Heart" is about "the relational pattern of choosing unavailable people and trying to get them to choose me back." The song captures the frenetic tension of that dynamic with its whimsical, unpredictable motion, flitting between folk sprawls and jazzy ascensions. At the same time, "Circadian Heart" refuses to fall into familiar cycles, snowballing into a cathartic release and soaring into the unknown. —Danielle

2

Bassvictim - "White Flag"

You wave the white flag to ask for peace. You're in a vulnerable position. You swallow your pride and ask how this whole mess can be resolved. Dido rejected it. She will go down with this ship, and she won't put her hands up and surrender. There will be no white flag above her door. She's in love and always will be. Bassvictim's Maria Manow, on the other hand, embraces it: "Your words got me fucked! I feel sick, go away! Words are swords! I don't fight, go away!" So why does Bassvictim's hammer-skitter lo-fi electroclash bleep-thump tantrum sound so much more warlike than anything Dido ever did in her entire life? —Tom

1

Cloud Nothings - "Death Keeps Me Alive"

I love Cloud Nothings. Though I admire their prolific, consistent discography, nothing has surpassed my love for their second album, Attack On Memory. It's raw and raucous, maintaining the perfect balance of gritty and clean. Yet "Death Keeps Me Alive," the lead single from the Cleveland band's new metal-inspired album What Kind of Hell Did You Survive?, might be the best thing they've ever done. The song takes the unhinged tumult of the Attack On Memory highlight "Wasted Days" and gives it a metallic edge that no one knew it needed. Cloud Nothings have been a band for almost two decades now, and they've finally unlocked the secret to revitalizing themselves: ferociousness. —Danielle

entry.title: Mark William Lewis – “Adrenaline”
entry.summary: We’ve made it to New Music Friday, which means Mark William Lewis, the baritone Briton who became the first signing to A24 Music, has released the deluxe edition of last year’s self-titled album. The expanded album adds five bonus tracks, four of which are firmly in the “bonus track” zone: Power Snatch’s cover of “Spit,”…
entry.content:
We've made it to New Music Friday, which means Mark William Lewis, the baritone Briton who became the first signing to A24 Music, has released the deluxe edition of last year's self-titled album. The expanded album adds five bonus tracks, four of which are firmly in the "bonus track" zone: Power Snatch's cover of "Spit," a "Still Above" remix by Taylor Skye, a dub version of "Petals" by the Mad Professor, and a live cut of "Ugly" from New York's Cherry Lane Theatre. But there is one new studio recording from Lewis in the bunch.

That song, "Adrenaline," maintains Williams' signature creeping, off-kilter vibe. It's so smooth it feels haunted, like King Krule making a Destroyer album or the National going new age. It won't rev you up like the title suggests, but it might quicken your breathing and raise your pulse without you realizing it. Listen below, where you can also find a stream of the full deluxe.

Mark William Lewis (Deluxe) is out now on A24 Music.

entry.title: Bottom Of The Hill Isn’t Closing After All
entry.summary: The small San Francisco venue Bottom Of The Hill has been a staple in the indie rock touring world for decades, so people were understandably bummed to learn that it was shutting down. Back in January, longtime owners Kathleen Owen, Ramona Downey, and Lynn Schwarz announced that 2026 would be the club’s final year. But…
entry.content:
The small San Francisco venue Bottom Of The Hill has been a staple in the indie rock touring world for decades, so people were understandably bummed to learn that it was shutting down. Back in January, longtime owners Kathleen Owen, Ramona Downey, and Lynn Schwarz announced that 2026 would be the club's final year. But now, it looks like Bottom Of The Hill will keep going under different ownership.

SFist reports that the biotech scientist Michele Bronson has bought the venue from Owen, Downey, and Schwarz and that she "reportedly plans to retain the existing staff and preserve the club’s reputation as an independent venue for emerging artists." The club will shut down for a month for needed kitchen renovations, as well as an update of its website and ticketing system." The previous owners were reportedly touched by the outpouring of love for the venue, and that's why they reconsidered their decision to close it rather than selling it.

According to SFist, Brunson moved to San Francisco to get a PhD in molecular biology in the early '90s, and she's been a regular at Bottom Of The Hill since the early '90s. Over the years, she has helped launch or run five biotech startups. The current owners will keep the property, as well as its upstairs apartments, while Brunson will take over the venue space and the name. She also plans to book the club herself, and she pledges to keep the club's policy of not taking a cut from the artists' merch money. She's looking into bringing back the Sunday barbecues that the venue used to host in its early years.

Before Brunson takes over, the current owners will say goodbye with a week-long run of shows at the end of the year, including appearances from indie veterans like Shannon Shaw, Man Or Astro-Man?, and Mark Eitzel.

entry.summary: Chappell Roan has spent the past two nights her own Super Graphic Spectacular Block Party benefit shows at LA’s Shrine Auditorium. On both nights, Roan took the opportunity to showcase and perform with some of her favorites. On night one, she brought out foundational superstar Christina Aguilera as a surprise guest. Aguilera sang her own…
entry.content:
Chappell Roan has spent the past two nights her own Super Graphic Spectacular Block Party benefit shows at LA's Shrine Auditorium. On both nights, Roan took the opportunity to showcase and perform with some of her favorites. On night one, she brought out foundational superstar Christina Aguilera as a surprise guest. Aguilera sang her own ballad "Beautiful" and then joined Roan for her own song "Coffee." The second night of the two-night extravaganza was Thursday night, and she had some more friends with her.

Last night's opening acts included MUNA and Caroline Polachek. Polachek only sang two songs, and one of them was her 2019 ballad "Look At Me Now." Midway through the song, Roan joined Polachek and turned it into a duet. The two of them looked and sounded luminous up there together.

During her own set, Chappell Roan also brought out PinkPantheress. Before introducing her guest, Roan said a lot of nice things about the direction in which she's taking pop music before gushing, "She's just so cunt!" Then PinkPantheress came out and sang a charming take on "Tonight." Roan didn't sing it with her as a duet or anything, but she did have fun with some of the call--and-response stuff at the end.

Lola Young was one of Chappell Roan's night-one openers. Last night, Roan sang her own big ballad "Picture You," and Young emerged mid-song to really belt out some of those parts.

I'm enjoying this "pop stars admiring and being friends with each other" dynamic. Let's keep that going.

entry.content:
The Singapore-born avant-pop artist yeule released their album Evangelic Girl Is A Gun last year. Earlier this year, they covered Nancy Sinatra for the performance art film in which they rolled around in paint. Today, they quietly share a new single called "Hystérique," distorted but glowingly romantic synthpop jam that reminds me of a long-gone version of Grimes.

"Hystérique" moves yeule closer to the realm of straight-up pop, though they're still nowhere near anyone's idea of the mainstream, even if their collaborators are. In this case, yeule co-wrote and co-produced "Hystérique" with Devin Workman and Chris Greatti, professional types who have collaborated, respectively, with Dominic Fike and Yungblud. Check it out below.

"Hystérique" is out now on Ether Eternal/Warner.

entry.title: Haute & Freddy – “Film Noir” & “In Your Eyes” (Peter Gabriel Cover)
entry.summary: Earlier this year, Haute & Freddy, the duo of big-deal pop songwriters Michelle Buzz and Lance Shipp, released Big Disgrace, a seriously fun album of theatrical, maximalist, big-personality pop music with heavy Chappell Roan/Lady Gaga vibes. The duo’s single “Touch Touch” followed in August. Right now, Haute & Freddy are getting a big boost from…
entry.content:
Earlier this year, Haute & Freddy, the duo of big-deal pop songwriters Michelle Buzz and Lance Shipp, released Big Disgrace, a seriously fun album of theatrical, maximalist, big-personality pop music with heavy Chappell Roan/Lady Gaga vibes. The duo's single "Touch Touch" followed in August. Right now, Haute & Freddy are getting a big boost from Mike Flanagan's new Prime Video adaptation of the Stephen King classic Carrie, so it's a great time to release another new single and to drop the Peter Gabriel cover that already appeared on the show.

As it happens, my wife and I finished watching Carrie last night. Pretty fun! I don't think it's anywhere near the level of Flanagan's old series Midnight Mass, which I consider to be a kind of masterpiece, but I had a good time with it. Flanagan has taken some big liberties with King's novel and Brian De Palma's beloved movie version. He has moved the story up to the present, and he has made some surprising adjustments. I don't think the twists were improvements or anything, but I was into them. If you're going to tell an old story again, you should switch it up and put your stamp on it. Flanagan nailed the casting and the finale, which are what matters the most when it comes to Carrie.

As previously noted, there is a lot of Haute & Freddy in Carrie. Flanagan says that the group's album helped inspire his version of the Carrie story, and he included eight of their songs. I liked Big Disgrace when it arrived in February, but I have listened to it a lot more since I started watching Carrie. So this is an ideal time for the duo to release "Film Noir," an '80s-style synthpop jam. Great song! in a press release, the duo says, "It should come as no shock to the royal court that we wanted our Halloween offering to feel as though the phantom himself created it. Though no mere mortal could ever wear his mask, we can always try to conjure as much drama and lust into 3:48 seconds." Amalia Irons directed the spooky-glammy black-and-white video.

As a digital B-side, Haute & Freddy have also shared their take on "In Your Eyes," the eternal teen-movie chestnut that Peter Gabriel released in 1986 and that found another life when John Cusack held up the Say Anything boom box three years later. Haute & Freddy's cover appears as diegetic music in the Carrie prom scene.

There's another new Haute & Freddy song, too. It's called "Do You Remember The Lilacs," and it also appeared in Carrie. Right now, though, it's an Amazon Music exclusive, so you're on your own there. I guess you'll just have to sign up for that streaming service to hear it. You shouldn't even bother checking for it anywhere else. Big Disgrace is out now on Atlantic.

entry.content:
One of the great lost media stories of the past decade is Panchiko, a band of British teenagers playing post-Radiohead alt-rock circa Y2K, whose one CD-R, 2000's self-released D>E>A>T>H>M>E>T>A>L, was plucked from obscurity and developed a very young, very online fanbase in the late 2010s. The members of Panchiko, who had long since moved on with their lives, learned about their cult following in 2020 and eventually reformed the band, releasing the comeback album Ginkgo in 2024. Now they've got another LP on deck.

Chimera will be out in April. It finds Panchiko once again collaborating with billy woods, who graced the Gingko single "Shandy In The Graveyard," as well as Cotillon, Hugh Pascall, Korea Girl, Abby Sage, Lula Nova, and CJ's Mirra Maze. There are also two collaborations with Clarion and three with the young indie jazz-pop Artist To Watch Mei Semones, including lead single "One Car Hits Another," out today.

Panchiko's Andy Wright offers some background on the song:

I imagined a serene waltz of a car crash, whilst onlookers and soon-to-be roadkill alike all sing along watching the slow motion collision unfold. A hand shake, or a car crash, the matter of fact news report describing the incident never makes it clear where the true devastation lies… one car hits another… one hand shakes another; they’re both meetings, technically.

Listen below.

entry.title: “World’s Top Autograph Seeker” Apologizes To Harry Styles After Heated Street Encounter
entry.summary: Right now, Harry Styles is in the middle of his massive 30-show residency at New York’s Madison Square Garden. That means that he sometimes has to walk around in New York, a place where he’ll get recognized even if he dons the standard celebrity hat/sunglasses disguise. (Styles and Thom Yorke recently commiserated about how it’s…
entry.content:
Right now, Harry Styles is in the middle of his massive 30-show residency at New York's Madison Square Garden. That means that he sometimes has to walk around in New York, a place where he'll get recognized even if he dons the standard celebrity hat/sunglasses disguise. (Styles and Thom Yorke recently commiserated about how it's better to walk around with the people.) Earlier this week, he got into what looked like an argument with an aggressive autograph seeker, and it made the news.

On Wednesday, Styles was out in the Manhattan streets, and he got into an on-camera dispute with someone who wanted him to sign a copy of his recent album Kiss All The Time. Disco, Occasionally. TMZ, reporting on the incident, called it a "heated exchange." Styles has a reputation for being gracious with fans, but this was not one of those situations. In the video, Styles never freaked out or anything, but he didn't seem happy with the guy, who kept following him when he tried to walk away.

The other guy in that conversation turns out to be someone named Giovanni, who refers to himself as "the world's top autograph seeker" in his Instagram bio. In a statement posted on Instagram last night, Giovanni apologized to Styles, saying the he was the one in the wrong in this situation:

Harry didn't lose his cool. I did. He stayed calm and even helped calm me down.

I want to clear up some of the headlines about my recent encounter with Harry Styles in NYC.

Harry has always been a gentleman to me, going all the way back to 2012 when he first signed for me.

The truth is, I was having a bad day and I was out of line. Harry was actually totally chill about the whole situation and even helped calm me down.

The headlines suggesting Harry lost his cool couldn't be further from the truth. If anything, I was the one who needed to cool down.

I take full responsibility and sincerely apologize to Harry. He's always been cool with me, and he deserves nothing but respect.

Well, that's nice. We can only hope that John Wilson will do something with all this. In other news, Spotify has announced plans to end Styles' MSG residency with "the ultimate Harryween celebration," which appears involve the return of LCD Soundsystem frontman James Murphy's old vinyl-only DJ night Despacio.

Also, Styles reportedly noticed Vogue boss Anna Wintour in the crowd at a recent show ant told her to "go to bed."

entry.title: Kacey Musgraves Announces Middle Of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes: Hear Two Tracks
entry.summary: Kacey Musgraves redirected her focus to her small-town Texas roots on this year’s excellent Middle Of Nowhere. One dimension of that exercise was an embrace of Tex-Mex sounds, including a dip into the regional Mexican subgenre Norteño on the Willie Nelson duet “Uncertain, TX” and performing shows with teenage mariachi musicians. Now she’s diving all…
entry.content:
Kacey Musgraves redirected her focus to her small-town Texas roots on this year's excellent Middle Of Nowhere. One dimension of that exercise was an embrace of Tex-Mex sounds, including a dip into the regional Mexican subgenre Norteño on the Willie Nelson duet "Uncertain, TX" and performing shows with teenage mariachi musicians. Now she's diving all the way into that sound on a Middle Of Nowhere companion album.

Out in January, Middle Of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes features 16 new tracks exploring the connection between Texas and Mexico. Musgraves sings four of those songs in Spanish, including a new version of "Uncertain, TX" with regional Mexican band Intocable subbing in for Nelson. Today she's sharing two preview tracks, "Weekend In Texas" and "Mi Tesoro."

"Weekend In Texas" infuses Musgraves' smart and snappy pop-country songwriting with persistent organ stabs and mariachi horns, and it plays on the same Texas/Tennessee rivalry that informs this year's biggest hit, "Choosin' Texas," cowritten by her nemesis-turned-friend Miranda Lambert. "I got everything I need/ So I'll Tennessee myself right out the door," she sings. "And spend the weekend in Texas/ With all the playboys and Bob Wills on the dance floor/ Tequila for breakfast/ Leave all my cares behind."

"Mi Tesoro," meanwhile, is a Norteño traditional sung in Spanish. I'm no native speaker, but it seems like Musgraves holds her own here. Decide below, where you can check out both tracks.

entry.title: The Black Parade Turns 20
entry.summary: You can’t just decide to make a classic album. If it were that easy, everyone would do it. We’d have to sort through piles of classic albums every week. An artist can’t simply make up their mind that their new album is about to be a classic. But one thing that artists can do is…
entry.content:
• Reprise
  • 2006

You can't just decide to make a classic album. If it were that easy, everyone would do it. We'd have to sort through piles of classic albums every week. An artist can't simply make up their mind that their new album is about to be a classic. But one thing that artists can do is try. They can put everything out there, hammering away at their own biggest ideas with all the resources available to them. That's a risky strategy. It doesn't work out often, and when it fails, the artist looks like a self-important fool. The conditions have to be exactly right. The artist has to be in the right place, mentally and temporally, to make something that will resonate and endure. In 2006, My Chemical Romance had the opportunity and the motive. They went for it, and they made it happen. They won.

I didn't think that My Chemical Romance's third and best album was a classic when it first came out. I resisted it. The Black Parade, which turns 20 on Saturday, came with a whole lot of advance hype. There would be strings on this album. Horns. Choirs. Liza Minelli. Visual themes. A grand, pretentious overarching storyline. The band invented whole new personas for themselves. They wore matching costumes and added theatrical props to their live show. Every night on tour, they played the entire record in full before digging back into their previous hits. During the pre-release press cycle, Gerard Way even cut his hair short and bleached it to embody the cancer-patient alter ego that he'd conjured for the record. (He was really imitating past generations of rockers inventing new looks for new albums. To the best of my knowledge, chemotherapy doesn't shorten your hair or turn it blonde.)

I was wrong about The Black Parade, and in the wake of the album's anniversary, I've caught myself wondering why. When The Black Parade came out, I'd just turned 27, which means I was about the same age as the members of the band, not their fans. Their fans were about a decade younger than any of us. They were the products of the mid-'00s MySpace emo boom, an easy scene to dismiss if you were a snarky aspiring rock critic in the mid-'00s. Two decades later, it's apparent that the MySpace emo boom was the last moment in history that guitar-based rock music could achieve cultural dominance amongst wide swaths of young people. We've had little rock-is-back rumbles since then, but nothing on the level of what MCR and their peers achieved in that moment. I had fun keeping tabs on that stuff at the time, but I should've paid better attention. This was an historic moment. We only get so many of those.

My Chemical Romance were around in the earliest days of the emo boom times, and they were by far the most theatrical band from that scene, at least until the actual theater dorks like Panic! At The Disco came along. The "Helena" video, with its smudged makeup and its Broadway choreography, seemed unbelievably silly, at least compared to the rap and indie rock stuff that I loved at the time. When I flipped over to Fuse and saw the girl jumping out of the coffin to dance, I laughed out loud. I let those fripperies distract me from an all-timer of a rock chorus. That's on me. Those fripperies were what drew so many kids to MCR, and the all-timer choruses were what made them stay. Or I don't know, maybe it's the other way around.

In any case, My Chemical Romance's 2004 major-label debut Three Cheers For Sweet Revenge went platinum, and then it sold another two million copies in intervening decades. Its success shoved MCR into the same conversations as the other Warped Tour bands that blew up among teenagers in that Web 2.0 era: Fall Out Boy, Taking Back Sunday, Hawthorne Heights, Thrice, the Starting Line, Brand New. My Chemical Romance couldn't wait to get out of those conversations.

The band came up on the New Jersey basement-emo circuit, and Thursday's Geoff Rickly, another rising star in that sudden emo explosion, produced their 2002 debut I Brought You My Bullets, You Brought Me Your Love. If that album had come out a few months earlier, I might've seen MCR at one of the same Syracuse hardcore matinee shows where I used to see Thursday. But My Chemical Romance didn't want to take the mutually supportive catharsis of those basement shows to the masses, the way Thursday did. They also didn't want to transform it into bright and glossy pop, like Fall Out Boy. They wanted to make a horns-blasting, flags-flying classic rock album of epic proportions.

When Gerard and Mikey Way were young boys, their father took them into the city to see the Smashing Pumpkins play Madison Square Garden on the Mellon Collie tour. When the brothers saw that, that's what they wanted to make. The Pumpkins' appetite for grandeur set them apart in the time of grunge, and My Chemical Romance had a similar relationship to the emo spaces from whence they sprang. They operated within the larger Warped Tour ecosystem, but that wasn't how they saw themselves. In Chris Payne's extremely readable emo oral history Where Are Your Boys Tonight?, Mikey Way says, "We wanted to be a rock band. At the time, we were at odds with the term 'emo,' and we did everything we could, kicking and screaming, to get away from it. Even if it meant risking everything."

When they made The Black Parade, My Chemical Romance risked everything. They went into the process with the clear intent of crafting a vast and ambitious concept album. The record's working title was The Rise And Fall Of My Chemical Romance, but they decided, quite sensibly, that this idea was too cute. Before any of the music was written, Gerard Way came up with the Black Parade title, as well as the mythology, the arc, and the aesthetic. Mikey says that Gerard "had costumes and characters immediately, just drawing them in his notebook." Maybe Green Day's similarly grandiose, genre-defying 2004 album American Idiot was a precedent, too. MCR toured with Green Day in 2005, and they enlisted that band's greatest collaborator, Rob Cavallo, as their Black Parade co-producer. When they started making videos for the album, MCR brought in "Smells Like Teen Spirit" director Samuel Bayer. Their choice of collaborators purposefully aligned them with the previous decade's alt-rock titans, not with their own jelly-bracelet peers.

MCR and Cavallo decamped to LA's famously spooky Paramour Mansion to record The Black Parade before they'd written almost anything, and they struggled through the sessions. Mikey Way, in particular, had a paralyzing fear of ghosts, and people love to talk about how that place is haunted. He developed night terrors so extreme that he had to take a mental-health break from the band. A newly sober Gerard threw himself into the writing process, coming up with an involved storyline about a dying man trying to make peace with his own regrets, inadequacies, and broken connections on the way out. Showbiz legend Liza Minnelli recorded a vocal cameo, probably more for symbolic presence than for actual vocal texture, though she did sing the hell out of her extremely brief part. Minnelli had never met the band, but she was happy to be included, and she did her work for free.

When the painstaking production process was finally complete, Rob Cavallo celebrated by renting a private jet and flying the band to Vegas, where they stayed at the Real World suite in the MGM Grand. That's not emo behavior, or least it hadn't been emo behavior until emo became big business. It's arena rock behavior. The truly cool thing about The Black Parade is that My Chemical Romance weren't just dressing up in arena rock drag. It's a righteously stirring over-the-top opus, way closer to Queen or Bowie or Guns N' Roses than the Promise Ring or Sunny Day Real Estate. MCR kept the frantic energy of their earlier records, and they translated it into something truly absurd and majestic. It's inspiring that they tried, and it's even more inspiring that they nailed it.

The Black Parade has the great rock-star combination of sincerity and irony, one of those classic situations where you can't tell where one ends and the other begins. When they play a blazing, soaring guitar solo, are they putting quotation marks around the blazing, soaring guitar solos from classic rock radio, or are they doing it for real? When Gerard Way brings a cheeky, sneery preen-snarl to his songs about love and death, is he distancing himself from his own words, or does that just come naturally to him? Does it matter? When I hear the tidal swells of melody on "I Don't Love You" today, I stop worrying about whether it's the obligatory power-ballad moment, and I just feel the power. This century has given us vanishingly few over-the-top power ballads on the level of "I Don't Love You." In the rare and miraculous case where a band has the clout and the inclination to put the necessary resources into the creation of a song like that, the listener must really stop fretting about intent.

I couldn't stop fretting about intent, and context, and whatever ideas of coolness I had in 2006. I was not prepared to take The Black Parade seriously when it came out, and I had to be like, "Damn, that's pretty good" when I finally heard it. But I wasn't a convert immediately. A few months after the record came out, I got together with some critic friends and trucked out to Long Island to see My Chemical Romance headline Nassau Coliseum, the vast hulk of a dilapidated arena that wasn't as close to New York City as I thought. The building wasn't full, but the kids who gathered for the MCR experience were all-in. Thousands upon thousands of teenagers wore skeleton-hands gloves, and there was so much Nightmare Before Christmas merch on display that you'd think Jack Skellington was an emo frontman — which, come to think of it, maybe he was. The kids of Long Island were there for a Hot Topic rock opera, and MCR delivered.

When I think back on that MCR show, it scarcely feels real — the Tim Burton-looking set, the matching costumes, the intro where stagehands wheeled Gerard Way out on a gurney. But when I read what I actually wrote in the moment, I see my own resistance at work, even the review was mostly positive: "My Chemical Romance isn’t an arena band, at least not yet; they’re still an emo band playing at an arena and pulling out every trick they know to convince us that they know what they’re doing... I couldn’t escape the nagging impression that MCR’s reach slightly exceeds its abilities." Maybe the decades have erased any awkwardness from my memory, or maybe I was just determined to hold back on my enthusiasm for a band that I still considered to be kids' stuff on some fundamental level.

There is some awkwardness in The Black Parade. The oompah affectations of "Mama" still grate on me 20 years later, and I can feel Gerard Way reaching a little too hard for majesty here and there. Maybe the concept itself was a crutch. Both then and now, my favorite song on The Black Parade is the one that exists entirely outside of the overarching narrative. "Teenagers" is a bitchy blast, a turbo-glam anthem with nothing to tell us about life and death. It's just a half-joking Gerard Way roaring that teenagers scare the living shit out of him over some of the stompingest riffs of 2006. That night on Long Island, the teenagers ate it up. If I have one real complaint about The Black Parade, it's that it could use more songs like "Teenagers."

Gerard Way said that he wrote "Teenagers" after finding himself on a New York subway car full of teenagers and realizing that they really did scare the living shit out of him. It got him thinking about his own not-that-distant teenage days and the adults that treated him as something less than human. It took forever to get back to Brooklyn the night after the Long Island show, and I vividly remembers all the teenagers who were on the train with me. They didn't scare me at all. I felt weirdly protective toward them. I had to take two or three trains to get back home that night, and the crowds of kids got smaller and smaller, but I could still tell who'd been at the show. By the time I reached my neighborhood, it was just me and a handful of Black and Latina girls in their skeleton-hand gloves. These kids defied the suburban mall-rebel image that I had for MCR fans, and maybe I should've thought a little harder about what their presence meant before writing that MCR weren't really an arena band.

But then, The Black Parade didn't necessarily feel like a momentous cultural moment when it first came out, at least to someone as prematurely washed as me. The album was a hit, certainly. In its first week, it sold more than 200,000 copies but debuted at #2 on the album chart, stuck behind the first Hannah Montana soundtrack. (I wonder how many kids bought both of those albums that week.) "Welcome To The Black Parade" became the band's first and only top-10 hit on the Hot 100. The Black Parade ultimately went quadruple platinum, which means it sold more than Three Cheers For Sweet Revenge, but not much more. The album got generally positive reviews, and a few critics really went to bat for it, but it didn't crack the top 40 on the year-end Pazz & Jop poll.

Right away, though, My Chemical Romance's peers knew that they'd all been lapped. In Where Are Your Boys Tonight?, there's a great moment where Taking Back Sunday's Fred Mascherino recalls the moment that MCR played The Black Parade for their Long Island peers: "Louder Now came out, and we're like, 'Oh man, we crushed this. No one can touch "Makedamnsure" or "My Blue Heaven!"' And then they played us Black Parade, and it's just like... motherfucker." Some of the press recognized The Black Parade as an event, too — the British vampires at the Daily Mail who published the alarmist trend-piece about "why no child is safe from the sinister cult of emo." That's dumber than fuck, but it's also a real sign of cultural impact.

All these years later, it's clearer than ever that The Black Parade is My Chemical Romance's masterpiece and that it's the one true opus to come out of emo's arena moment. (Sorry, but My Chemical Romance are forever bound to that moment, whether or not that's what they wanted.) The band only had one more album in them, 2010's Danger Days: The True Lives Of The Fabulous Killjoys, before they hung it up. Now, they're back together, and they once again play The Black Parade in full every night on tour. They're still not an arena band, though. They leapfrogged that. They're a stadium band now. If anyone deserves that stadium status, it's them. When you set out to make a classic album and you actually succeed, stadiums are where you belong.

entry.title: Billy Corgan Defends Friendship With Marilyn Manson, Compares Himself To Kanye West, And Explains Resentment Toward “The Hipster Writer Class”
entry.summary: It’s combative Billy Corgan interview time! Right now, Corgan’s band the Smashing Pumpkins — the the in the name seems to be important to Corgan — are experiencing a bit of a resurgence. Their ’90s hits are all over TikTok. They’re touring arenas to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Mellon Collie And The Infinite Sadness.…
entry.content:
It's combative Billy Corgan interview time! Right now, Corgan's band the Smashing Pumpkins — the the in the name seems to be important to Corgan — are experiencing a bit of a resurgence. Their '90s hits are all over TikTok. They're touring arenas to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Mellon Collie And The Infinite Sadness. They reunited with their Siamese Dream/Gish producer Butch Vig to record "Black Stars," a soundtrack song for the upcoming Hunger Games movie. Olivia Rodrigo performed with them at Lollapalooza. And now, Corgan is the latest guest on the New York Times Popcast. He's got some things that he'd like to say.

Corgan seems to relish the chance to go toe-to-toe with a coastal music critic like my friend Jon Caramanica and to ask him whether, in his own words, "Has my work been fairly assessed by your critical class?" Along the way, he veers into digressions about other divisive stars, including his '90s alt-rock peer Marilyn Manson. Corgan remains close to Manson years after many women accused Manson of sexual assault. Last year, Manson appeared at Corgan's birthday party, and the two of them posed for photos together. When Caramanica asked Corgan about that, Corgan said:

I think it's a valid question, and I think that ultimately, as a Christian person, you have to — how can I put it? You have to stand by your friends, but that doesn't mean you can't have an opinion, and it doesn't mean you're not critical. In his case, and I'm not here to adjudicate it, but the DA looked at the case for five years. In some cases, I knew personal things behind the scenes that are not in the public sphere.

I personally didn't feel that he was guilty with the things he was being charged with, and ultimately the fact that the DA didn't pursue — so basically, the person that I knew, and the way it all kinda went down, even though it was an elongated process, was commensurate with the person that I knew. You know what I mean? It all kinda lined up. But I wasn't there. I can't be there for everything. But I guess it's one of those things where I don't want the world to tell me who my friends are and who I should associate with. That's politically, socially.

And in Brian [Warner]'s case, we have a relationship that goes back close to 30 years. The other thing that people should know, and it gets lost in the gloss here, is Manson's wife Lindsay [Usich] is a twin, and her twin Ashley is married to James Iha of the Pumpkins. So Manson's basically a part of our family. There's a deeper set of relationships there. Plus, I knew Manson's parents. So I think anybody in that situation struggles with the accusations, the seriousness of the accusations. But again, I also knew the inside baseball of the case. I knew certain people who were involved.

So you make those evaluations. At the end of the day, I feel I've made the right determination, but if things had come out — Like, people have asked me privately, "Well, what happens if...?" And I'd say, "If he's guilty, or if anyone in that situation is guilty, they should go to jail."

Elsewhere in the interview, Caramanica brings up Corgan's fellow self-aggrandizing Chicago star Kanye West, someone with whom Caramanica has a long history. Caramanica says, "I hear a lot of Kanye in you," and Corgan asks, "Isn't it the other way around? I did come first. And by the way, when we were making Mellon Collie, Kanye was literally working one block down the street at the Gap." Corgan then talks about watching West's rise: "When I first saw his game, I thought, 'Was he influenced by the way I did this shit?' Because it was the same game — pick fights, do crazy shit. That game, the way I call it, is this cognitive dissonance game..."

At this point, Times reporter and Popcast co-host Joe Coscarelli mentions that Corgan went on Alex Jones' InfoWars before West did, and Corgan says, "Sure." Then, he goes right back to the point he was making:

But by creating the cognitive dissonance conversation, you have to choose, you understand? So when I ask you a question like, "Has my work been fairly assessed by your critical class?," it forces you to make a decision of my value. So as an artist, that's what I saw Kanye doing. It was like, "I'm gonna pick the fight and make you decide whether I'm a genius or not, whether I'm an idiot or not." That's what that game is. I wonder if he got that game from me, but maybe it was just in the water.

These are conversational jags. The main thing that Corgan seems interested in discussing, at least in this interview, is the "critical class" thing. He brings up Pitchfork many times. Here he is, for instance, talking about the revival of interest in the Pumpkins' music:

I’ve been very critical of, let’s call it the Pitchfork generation. When they sold out alternative ethos for pop domination — in essence, celebrating Rihanna as an alternative star and wiping Siouxsie [Sioux] off the map — that to me was the great betrayal of the alternative ethos. So suddenly, all the things that make alternative music so beautiful — the messiness, the uncomfortability, the dissonance, the out-of-tune guitars — it was like, "Nah, that’s just too messy. We don’t have time for that anymore. We want this perfect works where it all adds up to a perfect synth line." And a lot of good music came out. I like the music. But I was like, "How do we not fit into this anymore?"

Later on, Corgan gets into the engineered commercialism of pop music, and he brings up Pitchfork again:

You're old enough to remember when Pitchfork suddenly decided that it was OK to sell your song to a commercial... Before that, you would've been hung up on a cross as a sellout. The #1 word of the '90s was "authenticity." My favorite word, because who was defining it? Usually upper middle class white people from the East Coast telling me, who grew up in a fucking basement, what authenticity was.

When Caramanica mentions that Corgan keeps bringing up Pitchfork, Corgan says, "Don't do that." He continues:

It's a stand-in for the hipster writer class, which by the way I fought all through the '90s. The evolution of that class in the early 2000s was suddenly like, "OK, alternative music isn't shiny or bright enough, and we're gonna get a lot more clicks with Rihanna, and now we're gonna hold Rihanna up as an alternative star, and we're gonna get her all the glow of alternative and street culture without the same criticism."

In the YouTube version of the conversation, Popcast editors then put a bunch of mediocre Rihanna Pitchfork scores onscreen, a nice touch. Both hosts push back on that point in the moment, but Corgan continues, "Who did they hold up as a vision of mockery, OK? The guy sitting right here, OK? In the cultural turnover, which is to be expected, they turned everything that I stood for into a negative." He goes on to talk about the "horrible reviews" that the Pumpkins got in the '90s and refers to critics, not unfairly, as "a bunch of schlubby fucking guys."

And there's more! Here's the part where, I think, Corgan gets to the meat of his argument:

Generally speaking, your classes are fucking hypocrites. Again, I'm not trying to personalize it. This is a nice conversation. But I'm saying: You, the general lot of you, don't really believe what you pretend to believe. And the street-level value of a truly authentic and organic musician who came up from the ground is a lot more valuable than people who live in ivory towers truly understand.

That's what leads directly into the Kanye thing. On paper, the conversation probably reads a lot more contentious than it seems if you listen to the podcast or watch the video. As a card-carrying member of the hipster critic class (who has said nice things about the Pumpkins' music), I found the whole thing pretty fascinating. You can watch the full extended interview below or read the Times' selective transcript here. In the video, the Marilyn Manson stuff is around the 53:30 mark, and the Kanye talk comes in around 45:30.

entry.title: Adéla Makes Her Late Night TV Debut On Fallon
entry.summary: Arguably this year’s biggest breakout pop star is Adéla. The Slovakian former ballerina and Dream Academy dropout is a dedicated student of the art of pop stardom, and her debut album Prima has spun off a pair of extremely fun slow-rolling hits, the soul-looped, spoken-word R&B jam “Nicole Kidman” and “Ain’t In LA,” more or…
entry.content:
Arguably this year's biggest breakout pop star is Adéla. The Slovakian former ballerina and Dream Academy dropout is a dedicated student of the art of pop stardom, and her debut album Prima has spun off a pair of extremely fun slow-rolling hits, the soul-looped, spoken-word R&B jam "Nicole Kidman" and "Ain't In LA," more or less a clone of "We Can't Stop" by her childhood inspiration Miley Cyrus. The album tracks are worth hearing too.

Thursday on The Tonight Show, Adéla made her late night TV debut. Not only did she perform a medley of "Nicole Kidman" and "Ain't In LA," she first sat for an interview with Jimmy Fallon. Adéla told the host she mastered her American accent by studying Hannah Montana and old pop star interviews with Fallon himself, as described on Prima's opening track "KGB." She then invited Fallon to join her in performing her signature move, the swaggerina.

You can behold this moment and Adéla's performance below.

Fun stuff, but her lip synching could use some work!

entry.title: Ryan Gosling’s Spooky Indie Band Dead Man Bones Announce First New Music In 17 Years
entry.summary: Back in 2009, Ryan Gosling was an indie film star who’d dabbled in indie music. in the stretch of time between his leading roles in 2007’s Lars And The Real Girl and 2010’s Blue Valentine, Gosling got together with the musician Zach Shields and formed the spooky indie rock band Dead Man’s Bones. The group…
entry.content:
Back in 2009, Ryan Gosling was an indie film star who'd dabbled in indie music. in the stretch of time between his leading roles in 2007's Lars And The Real Girl and 2010's Blue Valentine, Gosling got together with the musician Zach Shields and formed the spooky indie rock band Dead Man's Bones. The group recorded their self-titled debut album with the Silverlake Conservatory Children's Choir backing them up, and they did a little touring around Halloween 2009. Dead Man's Bones were a very cool little curio of its era, and nobody really expected them to return. But now, Dead Man's Bones are coming back like Lazarus.

These days, Ryan Gosling is not an indie film star. He is about as mainstream as movie stars get. His most recent picture, Project Hail Mary, is one of the year's biggest. His next two efforts are a Star Wars movie, Starfighter, and a Marvel movie, Ghost Rider. Even as a musician, Gosling is in a different realm now; he reached the pop charts a few years ago, when he sang "I'm Just Ken" in Barbie. So the return of Dead Man's Bones is a cool, welcome surprise. The group made the big announcement in a social media video yesterday: New music coming Oct. 27, just in time for Halloween. The teaser video is appropriately spooky.

The label ANTI- posted the video, too, so it looks like they'll release whatever's coming, just as they did with that self-titled album in 2009. When Stereogum's Instagram posted about the announcement last night, our commenters were unanimous in their approval, which never happens. On her own Instagram last night, Gosling's partner Eva Mendes posted the teaser video with this caption: "He came through on his promise to me." Perhaps we have her to thank.

Before the announcement, Redditors noticed that Gosling and Mendes' stylist Mark Avery was posting about "Dead Man's Bones on Halloween."

When Ryan Gosling was promoting Barbie in 2023, one interviewer asked him about the possibility of a Dead Man's Bones revival, and he said, "Maybe. Never say never?" NME also got Gosling talking about the band when he was promoting Project Hail Mary earlier this year.

entry.title: Raye Wins 2026 Mercury Prize
entry.summary: Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for This Music May Contain Hope. The award recognizes one album from the UK and Ireland every year with a panel of music industry figures determining its recipient. The award comes with a £25,000 prize. The panel praised “the scale, structure, ambition, and sheer charm” of Raye’s album,…
entry.content:
Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for This Music May Contain Hope. The award recognizes one album from the UK and Ireland every year with a panel of music industry figures determining its recipient. The award comes with a £25,000 prize.

The panel praised "the scale, structure, ambition, and sheer charm" of Raye's album, noting, "Raye displays real imagination and scope in showing what an album can be, going beyond any one style or genre to realise her vision. The judges agreed that Raye’s superb album will serve as a huge inspiration for years to come."

This year's other nominees were Dave for The Boy Who Played The Harp, Dove Ellis for Blizzard, Florence + The Machine for Everybody Scream, Jade for That’s Showbiz, Baby!, Knats for A Great Day In Newcastle, Kojey Radical for Don’t Look Down, Nia Archives for Emotional Junglist, Olivia Dean for The Art Of Loving, Paul McCartney for The Boys Of Dungeon Lane, Suede for Antidepressants, and various artists for the War Child compilation Help(2).

The ceremony took place at Utilita Arena in Newcastle upon Tyne, UK with performances from the nominees. Last year's Mercury Prize went to Sam Fender for People Watching.

As the BBC notes, the judges on this year's panel included the following: Afrodeutsche (composer, DJ, BBC Radio 3 and Radio 6 broadcaster), Danielle Perry (broadcaster and musician), Jamie Cullum (musician and BBC Radio 2 broadcaster), Lea Stonhill (music programming consultant), MistaJam (songwriter, DJ, and broadcaster) Phil Alexander, (creative director at Kerrang! and contributing editor for Mojo), Sian Eleri (BBC Radio 1 broadcaster and DJ), Sophie Williams (music writer and broadcaster), Will Hodgkinson (chief rock and pop critic for The Times), and Jeff Smith (head of music for BBC Radio 2 and BBC Radio 6 Music).

Raye was among the night's performers, singing the jazzy "I Hate The Way I Look Today." Watch her performance below.

Raye is set to make her acting debut in Yann Demange's thriller Lineage. Hopefully the Mercury panel heard the final mix of her album.

entry.title: Charli XCX Cast In Martin Scorsese’s What Happens At Night Alongside Leonardo DiCaprio & Jennifer Lawrence

entry.content:
Alongside music guy John Cale and fashion guy Marc Jacobs, Martin Scorsese represented motion pictures on the cover of Charli XCX's new album Music, Fashion, Film. (Charli herself joins in on the special edition CD cover, viewable above.) Now he's added the pop star to the cast of his upcoming movie.

Charli will add to her suddenly prolific list of acting roles by appearing in Scorsese's What Happens At Night, Variety reports. Apple and StudioCanal are producing the film, which stars Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence as a married couple who travel to a small European town to adopt a baby, then hit some snags that send them into a state of dark confusion.

Mads Mikkelsen, Patricia Clarkson, and Jared Harris are also in the movie, which has been described as a Gothic psychological horror film. Charli's role has not been revealed, but when it comes to babies, she thinks about it all the time.

entry.title: Natalie Bergman Announces New EP I Killed A North American Songbird: Hear “White Oak”
entry.summary: Natalie Bergman from Wild Belle has been carving out a solo career in the 2020s. My Home Is Not In This World, her album for Third Man Records last year, presented an immensely pleasant blend of retro pop, soul, and folk sounds. It bodes well for I Killed A North American Songbird, the new EP…
entry.content:
Natalie Bergman from Wild Belle has been carving out a solo career in the 2020s. My Home Is Not In This World, her album for Third Man Records last year, presented an immensely pleasant blend of retro pop, soul, and folk sounds. It bodes well for I Killed A North American Songbird, the new EP she announced today — as if that title alone was not enough to pique your interest.

The five-song project will be out in a couple weeks. Bergman is teasing it today with a video for "White Oak," the opening track. Produced by Ben Lumsdaine, it's a woozy, off-kilter soul ballad, a song where retro sounds are manipulated in thoroughly modern ways. "Alone in the wilderness/ You were born to make beautiful things," Bergman sings. "We laid his body in the ground/ You played the melody on baritone."

Andreas Ekelund directed the "White Oak" video, which stars dancers Staz Lindes, Sandi Denton, and June Tate. Watch below.

TRACKLIST:
01 "White Oak"
02 "Indigo Bunting"
03 "Disappearing"
04 "The Way That You Love Me"
05 "Peregrine Falcon"

I Killed A North American Songbird is out 11/6 on Third Man. Pre-order it here.

entry.title: Zelooperz Announces New Album Pin Breakers: Hear “Beautician”
entry.summary: The Detroit rap expressionist Zelooperz and the avant-rap producer Black Noi$e have done a whole lot of work together over the years, and they’re about to release a lost album that they recorded almost a decade ago. Zelooperz and Black Noi$e started working together in 2017, when both of them were living at the Bruiser…
entry.content:
The Detroit rap expressionist Zelooperz and the avant-rap producer Black Noi$e have done a whole lot of work together over the years, and they're about to release a lost album that they recorded almost a decade ago. Zelooperz and Black Noi$e started working together in 2017, when both of them were living at the Bruiser House, the home base for Danny Brown's Bruiser Brigade crew. Over two years, they recorded a full collaborative album that they finished in 2019, but then they lost the hard drive where they'd been keeping it. Black Noi$e has since recovered that hard drive, and the resulting album, entitled Pin Breakers, comes out next month.

Pin Breakers gets its title from a shoulder injury that Black Noi$e suffered at a Glendale bowling alley, and it's Zelooperz' first release for Earl Sweatshirt's Tan Cressida label. There's only one guest on the record, and that's Danny Brown. Lead single "Beautician" is a hazy boom-bap workout that's full of personality even though it's barely longer than one minute. Check it out below.

entry.title: Jorja Smith, Corinne Bailey Rae, FLO, & More Cover Amy Winehouse With Mark Ronson At Back To Black 20 Tribute
entry.summary: Next Tuesday, Amy Winehouse’s classic breakout album Back To Black will celebrate its 20th anniversary, and there’s already a lot of hullabaloo around it, as you’d expect. Today, Variety reports that veteran Broadway producer Catherine Schreiber is developing an Amy Winehouse musical for London’s West End. (The biopic didn’t work, but who knows, maybe this…
entry.content:
Next Tuesday, Amy Winehouse's classic breakout album Back To Black will celebrate its 20th anniversary, and there's already a lot of hullabaloo around it, as you'd expect. Today, Variety reports that veteran Broadway producer Catherine Schreiber is developing an Amy Winehouse musical for London's West End. (The biopic didn't work, but who knows, maybe this will.) And on Tuesday night, Back To Black producers Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi led an all-star Back To Black tribute at London's Roundhouse.

At the Roundhouse show, Ronson and Remi joined a group of Amy Winehouse's stylistic descendants to cover every song from Back To Black. Corinne Bailey Rae sang the title track. Yabba did "Love Is A Losing Game." Lianne La Havas took on "You Know I'm No Good." Jorja Smith belted out "Some Unholy War." The London girl group FLO delivered their version of "He Can Only Hold Her," and "Rehab" duties went to Jessie Reyez. At the end of the night, all of the artists got together onstage for a group singalong of "Valerie," the Zutons song that Winehouse turned into a hit.

The BBC will broadcast the tribute show on its YouTube channel Saturday evening, and it'll air Oct. 26 on BBC Radio 2 and BBC Sounds. But since there were people in the crowd with phones, so you can already watch some lower-quality videos from the show below.

entry.summary: It was revealed last week that Druski would become the first online content creator to host SNL on Nov. 7. Now, we know that the Strokes will serve as the musical guest for that episode. We also now know that the following episode, slated for Nov. 14, will have John Mulaney as host and Phoebe…
entry.content:
It was revealed last week that Druski would become the first online content creator to host SNL on Nov. 7. Now, we know that the Strokes will serve as the musical guest for that episode. We also now know that the following episode, slated for Nov. 14, will have John Mulaney as host and Phoebe Bridgers as the musical guest.

The Strokes — who released their seventh record Reality Awaits earlier this year — have played SNL a few times, the latest of which was in 2020 with Mulaney hosting. Bridgers last played SNL with boygenius in 2023. Before that, she did a solo performance in 2020 and smashed her guitar, which made a lot of people, including David Crosby, irrationally angry. Bridgers just released her phenomenal third album Lost Weekend and has been bringing it to stages on her phone-free tour.

Previously, we knew that the Oct. 31 episode would have Obsession's Inde Navarette as host and Gracie Abrams as the musical guest.
